title_prefix: The per-peer tx announcement queue silen
mechanism: Core's per-peer send queue is std::set<Wtxid> m_tx_inventory_to_send: PushTxInventory inserts in logarithmic time (refs/bitcoin/src/net_processing.cpp:2261-2263) and NOTHING ever truncates it. It is drained in SendMessages (:6028-6086) with broadcast_max = INVENTORY_BROADCAST_TARGET + (m_tx_inventory_to_send.size()/1000)*5, capped at INVENTORY_BROADCAST_MAX (:6046-6047), so the drain accelerates as the backlog grows: 70 at rest, 95 at a 5,000-entry backlog, up to 1,000 (constants at :172-178, INVENTORY_BROADCAST_TARGET = INVENTORY_BROADCAST_PER_SECOND 14 x INBOUND_INVENTORY_BROADCAST_INTERVAL 5s = 70). Ours (src/networking/protocol.lisp:2873-2919) keeps a Lisp LIST: relay-transaction nconc's the new entry onto the tail, walking the whole list, then calls (length ...) on it, walking it again, and when the result exceeds +max-tx-inv-queue+ = 5000 (:2859) nthcdr's the excess off the FRONT -- the oldest queued announcements are discarded. %flush-peer-tx-invs (:3027-3072) drains a fixed +inv-broadcast-target+ = 70 (:2854) per pass with no backlog scaling. Nothing re-queues a discarded entry: relay-transaction is the only enqueue path for third-party transactions (the unbroadcast reattempt covers only locally submitted ones), so an entry dropped at the cap is never announced to that peer.
consequence: Announcements are silently lost, not delayed. Measured: 5,100 relay-transaction calls to one peer produced exactly 5,000 announcements, and the 100 oldest were never announced at all. Reaching the cap needs sustained accepted-transaction inflow above the drain rate -- 70 per ~2 s outbound (35/s) and per ~5 s inbound (14/s) -- which real fee spikes exceed, so an inbound peer's queue can fill in about a minute at 100 tx/s inflow; Core in the same conditions only lags and then catches up faster. The affected peer still learns the transaction from its other peers, from a BIP35 mempool request, or from us if it later asks, so no transaction leaves the network and our own mempool is unaffected. Filling the queue is not free for an attacker either: it requires fee-paying transactions our mempool accepts at a rate we cannot be forced into. The list representation costs two full walks of the queue per relayed transaction per peer -- measured 0.48 ms per relayed transaction across 8 peers at cap depth versus 0.0 ms with empty queues, i.e. about 0.06 ms per peer per transaction at depth 5,000, a clean O(n) signature but a small absolute cost. Bounded inefficiency plus a degraded-relay window, no censorship lever a peer controls outright: S3.
evidence: Probes ga11-txrelay-inv-queue and ga11-txrelay-flush-order (scripts/dev.sh load + eval), warm image bitcoin-lisp-sbcl:2.6.5-4. (1) Control: (:QUEUE-LEN-AFTER-10 10 :FIRST-ENTRY-IS-TX0 T) -- the queue grows one entry per relayed transaction and the head is the oldest. (2) Cap behaviour, 5,100 distinct txids to one peer: (:CAP 5000 :QUEUE-LEN 5000 :OLDEST-SURVIVING-INDEX 100 :NEWEST-SURVIVING-INDEX 5099 :TX0-STILL-QUEUED NIL :TX99-STILL-QUEUED NIL) -- pinned at the cap, survivors are indices 100..5099, so the OLDEST are the ones discarded. (3) The loss is permanent: draining the whole queue through %flush-peer-tx-invs gave (:TOTAL-ANNOUNCED 5000 :RELAY-CALLS 5100 :TX0-EVER-ANNOUNCED NIL :TX99-EVER-ANNOUNCED NIL :TX100-EVER-ANNOUNCED T :PER-FLUSH 70). (4) Cost: (:PEERS 8 :MS-PER-RELAYED-TX-QUEUE-EMPTY 0.0 :MS-PER-RELAYED-TX-QUEUE-AT-CAP 0.48 :DEEP-QUEUE-LEN 5000). (5) Drain comparison: (:OURS-FLUSH-TARGET 70 :CORE-BROADCAST-MAX-AT-CAP 95 :CORE-BROADCAST-MAX-AT-70 70). Ours: src/networking/protocol.lisp:2854, :2859, :2873-2919, :3027-3072. Core at d3056bc: refs/bitcoin/src/net_processing.cpp:172-178, :2250-2264, :6028-6086.
fix_shape: Replace the list with a structure that has Core's two properties: cheap insertion and no truncation. A per-peer hash table keyed by txid (already the de-duplication key the flush uses) alongside a tail-pointer queue, or an ordered structure if the fee-rate drain of finding 490e6e59 lands at the same time, removes both full walks and makes the queue depth irrelevant to relay cost. Then delete the nthcdr truncation: Core has no cap on m_tx_inventory_to_send at all, and the pressure valve it uses instead is the accelerating drain -- port broadcast_max = +inv-broadcast-target+ + (queue-length/1000)*5, clamped to an INVENTORY_BROADCAST_MAX of 1000 (net_processing.cpp:6046-6047), into %flush-peer-tx-invs so a backlog is worked off rather than thrown away. If a hard bound is still wanted as a memory guard, it must be far above MAX_PEER_TX_ANNOUNCEMENTS and it must drop the NEWEST entries or refuse the insert, never silently discard announcements the flush has already promised nothing about; note that Core's own static_assert at net_processing.cpp:178 ties INVENTORY_BROADCAST_MAX to MAX_PEER_TX_ANNOUNCEMENTS, so any cap chosen here should be justified against those two constants rather than picked independently.
